blocks.text: CHAPTER TWENTY- SEVEN APPROACH TO COMMON NEONATAL CONDITIONS
Common neonatal conditions are a major cause of illness and death in the first 28 days of life. Early recognition and prompt management are essential to improve survival and prevent complications.

runs.text: Common neonatal conditions are a major cause of illness and death in the first 28 days of life. Early recognition and prompt management are essential to improve survival and prevent complications.

blocks.text: Assessment begins with rapid identification of emergency signs including respiratory distress, apnoea, shock, convulsions, severe bleeding, hypothermia, poor feeding, and altered consciousness. Immediate management should follow the principles of airway, breathing, circulation, correction of hypoglycemia, and thermal protection.

blocks.text: A focused history should include maternal risk factors, antenatal and intrapartum events, gestational age, birth weight, feeding history, and any history of delayed cry or resuscitation. Physical examination should assess vital signs, respiratory status, hydration, jaundice, signs of infection, congenital abnormalities, and neurological status.

blocks.text: Investigations are guided by clinical findings and may include blood glucose, full blood count, C-reactive protein, blood culture, serum bilirubin, electrolytes, and relevant imaging.

runs.text: culture, serum bilirubin, electrolytes, and relevant imaging.

blocks.text: Management involves supportive care (warmth, oxygen, fluids, nutrition, and glucose correction) and specific treatment for conditions such as neonatal sepsis, neonatal jaundice, respiratory distress syndrome, birth asphyxia, and neonatal seizures.

runs.text: Management involves supportive care (warmth, oxygen, fluids, nutrition, and glucose correction) and specific treatment for conditions such as neonatal sepsis, neonatal jaundice, respiratory distress syndrome, birth asphyxia, and neonatal seizures.

blocks.text: Continuous monitoring and follow-up are essential for early detection of complications and improved outcomes.

Table 27.1 Emergency Signs Assessment and Immediate Management in Neonates
Place newborn on a warm surface under good light
Position airway in neutral position to maintain patency
Resuscitate using bag and mask ventilation if breathing is inadequate
Provide appropriate respiratory support to maintain SpO₂ 90–94%
Stop visible bleeding: → Umbilical stump: re-clamp/re-tie
→ Wound/cut site: apply sterile gauze compression
: Phytomenadione (Vitamin K₁) 2 mg IV stat (continue for 3 days if bleeding persists)
Send blood for grouping, cross-match, and coagulation profile
Establish IV access (intraosseous access if IV unavailable)
Send investigations: FBP, CRP, blood group, cross-match
A: sodium lactate (Ringer’s lactate) (IV )10–20 mL/kg over 15–20 minutes
D: packed red blood cells (PRBCs) 20 mL/kg transfusion
If RBG <2.6 mmol/L OR unable to measure:
A: phenobarbitone (IV/IM) 20 mg/kg slowly over 20 minutes
Perinatal asphyxia is failure to initiate and sustain breathing after delivery and/or APGAR score of <7 in the 5th minute.

This is a serious systemic condition of infectious origin occurring in the first month of life. Neonatal sepsis is classified as early- onset or late onset.
It is diagnosed in the first 3 days and caused by pathogens in the mother’s genital tract.
27.2 Risk factors and clinical indicators for early-onset neonatal sepsis
Red Flags (High Risk – urgent admission & evaluation)
Non–Red Flags (Warning signs – close observation & assessment)
Suspected or confirmed infection in twin (multiple pregnancy)
Previous baby with Group B Streptococcal (GBS) infection
Respiratory distress beginning after 4 hours of age (suggests pathology rather than transition)

runs.text: hours of age (suggests pathology rather than

blocks.text: Vomiting, high gastric aspirates, abdominal distension
Central cyanosis or low oxygen saturation
Red flags → immediate admission, full sepsis work-up, and urgent management
Non–red flags → close monitoring, reassessment, and early intervention if progression occurs
Neonate ≤ 3days to be investigated for sepsis and started on antibiotics:
Those with any red flag risk factor or clinical indicator
Those with 2 or more none red flag risk factor or clinical indicator
Lumbar puncture (in case of CNS signs)
Chest X-ray (in case of respiratory signs)
Management of early-onset neonatal sepsis Start antibiotics immediately (do not wait for results) A: ampicillin (IV) 50 mg/kg 12 hourly for 5 – 7 days
A: gentamicin (IV) 5 mg/kg (3mg/kg for LBW neonates) 24hourly for 5 – 7 days
Provide other supportive care as indicated by the neonate’s condition
Close monitoring of vitals - respiratory rate, temp, SPO2, heart rate, RBG, BP and urine output
Late-onset sepsis is diagnosed after 3 days of age and is horizontally acquired from the environment and the people handling the neonate.

runs.text: and the people handling the neonate.

blocks.text: Table 27.3 Clinical indicators of possible late-onset neonatal sepsis
Not waking or not staying awake when aroused
Oxygen saturation <90% in room air or increased oxygen requirement
Persistent heart rate >160 bpm or <100 bpm (unexplained)
As described for early-onset sepsis Plus:
Lumbar puncture if there is no contraindication
Consider ABG (some babies have inborn error of metabolism and mistaken for sepsis)
All neonates with signs suggestive of sepsis need to be admitted for close observation
After taking samples for investigation commence antibiotics immediately
B: ampicillin + cloxacillin (FDC) (IV) 100 mg/kg 12hourly for 5 – 7 days
Monitor vitals continuously for neonates with severe clinical signs
Repeat septic markers (CRP) after 48hours of antibiotics
For treatment guidance regularly review the clinical condition and investigation results of the neonate
When to consider changing antibiotics to the next line for neonate with sepsis
If no clinical improvement after 48 hours of treatment
If culture results indicate resistance to current antibiotics

Low Birth Weight neonates (LBW) are at higher risk of early growth retardation, infections, developmental delay, impaired respiration, difficulty in feeding, poor body temperature regulation and death. The smaller the neonate, the higher the risk.

runs.text: impaired respiration, difficulty in feeding, poor body temperature regulation and death. The smaller the neonate, the higher the risk.

blocks.text: Table 27.4: Classification of Low-birth weight in neonates
Use radiant warmers with servo control mode
Ensure correct placement of temperature probe (right side, ~3 cm below right costal margin)
If probe failure → use manual mode and monitor axillary temperature every 15–30 minutes
In cold environments use heaters; in hot environments use air conditioning
Rewarm hypothermic neonates slowly (0.5°C/hour) to avoid complications
Start with Minimal Enteral Feeding (MEF / trophic feeds) when appropriate
Gradually advance feeds based on tolerance
Monitor feeding tolerance and abdominal distension
Use enteral feeding whenever possible before IV nutrition
Monitor temperature, weight, and feeding tolerance
Observe for signs of infection (treat only if indicated)
Monitor for respiratory distress and hypoglycemia
Note: Non-pharmacological care is the cornerstone of LBW management, especially thermal regulation, feeding support, and close monitoring.

runs.text: Non-pharmacological care is the cornerstone of LBW management, especially thermal regulation, feeding support, and close monitoring.

Gastrointestinal failure or inability to feed enterally
Gastrointestinal anomalies (gastroschisis, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, esophageal/intestinal atresia)
NPO neonates with no expected enteral feeds within 72 hours
<28 weeks (<1000 g): if no adequate feeds within 24 hours
28–32 weeks (1000–1500 g): if no adequate feeds within 3 days
>32 weeks (>1500 g): if no adequate feeds within 5 days
Ampicillin + Gentamicin remains first-line empirical therapy for suspected neonatal sepsis
Duration is typically 5–7 days, adjusted by clinical and microbiological response
TPN is indicated when enteral feeding is not possible or significantly delayed
Early nutrition improves survival and growth outcomes in LBW neonates
Calculate the total fluid intake (TFI) using birth weight then minus the amount of milk required for that day (if it exceeds trophic feed), and give the remaining amount as IV fluids over 24 hours.

blocks.text: Table 27.5: Total fluid requirement according to Birth weight and postnatal age
Things to consider when giving IV fluids
Type of fluid in the first 48 hours of life is Dextrose 10%
4/5 (80%) of total volume will be dextrose 10% the remaining 1/5 (20%) iv sodium chloride or sodium lactate
IV fluids should be given as a continuous infusion for 24 hours NOT bolus (preferably use an infusion pump if available).
Consider to stop IV fluid if neonate can take 2/3rd of total fluid required enterally and maintains normal RBG.

Apnoea of Prematurity is defined as a pause in breathing ≥20 seconds, or a shorter pause associated with bradycardia, cyanosis, or oxygen desaturation in preterm neonates due to immature respiratory control.

Table 27.7: Management of Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS)
PEEP: 6 cmH₂O Adjust FiO₂ and PEEP according to severity of respiratory distress and oxygen saturation.
Kangaroo Mother Care (intermittent skin-to-skin contact where appropriate)
If unable to feed, initiate IV fluids as per neonatal fluid guidelines
Administer if ALL of the following are present:
PEEP requirement ≥7 cmH₂O to maintain oxygen saturation ≥90%

blocks.text: Consider mechanical ventilation if: Severe respiratory distress:
Persistent oxygen saturation <90% after second dose of surfactant
Recurrent apnoea: More than two episodes within 24 hours
Refer promptly to a higher-level facility when:
Surfactant therapy is required but unavailable
Severe prematurity/low birth weight requiring specialized care
District Hospital and above: Sick neonates and/or neonates <1.8 kg
Start IV fluids if dehydrated or in shock
For gastroschisis: provide rehydration fluids as per neonatal fluid guidelines
Insert NGT for decompression where indicated
Maintain glucose through breastfeeding, NGT feeding, or IV fluids as appropriate
